newsitem.title: UK: Mowlam brings fighting spirit to N.Ireland brief.
newsitem.headline: Mowlam brings fighting spirit to N.Ireland brief.

text.p: Marjorie "Mo" Mowlam, named on Saturday as Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, brings a fighting spirit to a job fraught with some of the world's more intractable problems.
As the first woman to hold the job -- 10 men before her have failed to bring a lasting peace to the British-ruled province -- Mowlam, 47, has enjoyed a rapid rise through Labour ranks.

She recently hit the headlines when it was disclosed she had suffered a benign brain tumour, forcing Britain's tabloid press to backtrack on catty stories about her sudden weight gain and new hairstyle and instead applaud her quiet bravery.
Her brief in office: to bring peace to Northern Ireland, where the Irish Republican Army has been fighting to end British rule for more than a quarter of a century.

Peace talks initiated under the Conservative government of John Major, which was soundly defeated in the polls on Thursday, failed to seal a lasting settlement and offered no apparent prospect of a real breakthrough after the IRA resumed its campaign of violence in 1996.
In opposition, Labour joined forces with the Conservatives to maintain a united front on Northern Ireland and provide no divisions that could be exploited by the guerrillas.
In office, Mowlam will be working hard to bring about a new IRA ceasefire in the hope of reviving the peace talks.
Her strong ties with the United States, key players in the stalled peace process, could serve her well.

Mowlam came to politics in 1987, when she won the coastal seat of Redcar in northern England, following her first career as a lecturer in social anthropology at universities in Britain and the United States.

Her political career has been marked by a series of rapid promotions. A year after entering parliament, she was given a pivotal role in Labour's offensive to win over a wary financial sector, traditionally a bastion of Conservative support.
Since then Mowlam has spoken from the opposition frontbench on issues ranging from women's rights to National Heritage but it was on Northern Ireland that she made her mark.
Mowlam studied social anthropology at Durham University in northern England and gained a doctorate from Iowa University.

She has never been afraid to express her views and encountered controversy when she suggested Buckingham Palace, Queen Elizabeth's London residence, should be sold and the royal family re-housed in a stylish apartment.
She lists her favourite song as Lou Reed's "Walk on the Wild Side" and listens to Pink Floyd and Oasis. Her hobbies include swimming and watching football.
Last year, she married merchant banker Jon Norton.
